ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial video-call style with mostly short to medium turns outside the presentations, including frequent greetings, technical check-ins, and light small talk. Speakers use many fillers, repetitions, repairs, and false starts (“um,” “yeah,” repeated words, self-corrections), especially among non-native speakers, giving it an unpolished, spontaneous feel. The formal presentation segments are long and structured, but still conversational and hedged, with phrases such as “I think,” “we’re interested in,” “it could be,” and “what we think is.” Questions are generally polite and exploratory rather than adversarial, often prefaced with praise or disclaimers like “naive question” or “very good question”; challenges are indirect, framed as alternative possibilities or requests for clarification. Participants build on prior remarks by referencing a point just made, offering related examples, and acknowledging answers with brief “okay,” “right,” or “thanks.” Overlap and interruption are occasional but mild, mainly during handoffs, clarification, or enthusiastic follow-ups rather than conflict.

Meeting style for this meeting (quick_checkin): A rushed weekly check-in. People give short status updates and ask each other quick questions. Most turns are one or two sentences. Nobody summarizes. Someone has another meeting soon and the conversation stops where it stops.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Okay, so, quick one from me- the export finished last night, mostly.
  - Mostly?
  - Two of the sites didn't come through. I haven't looked yet.
Opening: Start with someone saying what they most want out of this meeting, briefly and casually.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Choosing which retrofits to fund so older apartment buildings stay safe during multi-day heat waves.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: Dr. Chen has 14 years of experience in building-performance engineering, including field audits and calibrated simulation of occupied multifamily buildings. She has led municipal resilience studies using EnergyPlus, submeter data, utility interval-load records, and indoor temperature sensor deployments, with particular attention to pre-1980 envelope conditions and electrical-service constraints.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She frames the funding choice as a coupled thermal-safety and electrical-capacity problem. For each of the six buildings, she will model apartment operative temperatures across three- to five-day heat waves, compare insulation, shading, cooling, and panel-upgrade packages, and estimate coincident peak demand and circuit/panel limitations. She emphasizes that a measure is not viable if modeled cooling equipment cannot be safely powered or if envelope changes produce negligible indoor-temperature protection during the critical heat period.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language

speakers.name: Dr. Amina Patel
speakers.background: Dr. Patel is an environmental epidemiologist with 11 years of experience studying heat exposure among older adults and renters in urban neighborhoods. Her work combines resident surveys, administrative emergency-department data, cooling-center utilization records, age-stratified vulnerability assessment, and quasi-experimental evaluation of housing and heat-protection interventions.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She treats indoor overheating as a preventable exposure pathway whose importance depends on resident vulnerability and access to alternatives. She will specify health-risk indicators and pilot outcomes using age distribution, reported cooling-center use, and heat-related emergency visits, while defining how changes in modeled apartment temperatures can be translated into exposure-relevant risk strata. She insists that the program be judged by whether high-risk residents can remain safely housed during heat waves, not solely by aggregate temperature reductions.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Daniel Okafor
speakers.background: Dr. Okafor is a postdoctoral researcher in applied urban and energy economics with five years of experience evaluating residential energy-efficiency and utility-affordability programs. He uses lifecycle cost models, distributional-incidence analysis, electricity-tariff data, stated-preference surveys, and benefit-cost frameworks that monetize avoided health events while distinguishing owner capital costs from tenant operating costs.
speakers.distinct_perspective: He frames retrofit funding as an allocation and incidence problem rather than a simple least-cost technology choice. He will calculate lifecycle and upfront costs, operating-cost changes, cost per avoided illness, and the distribution of electricity-bill impacts between landlords and tenants under different lease and metering arrangements. His key criterion is that cooling-oriented measures should not create an affordability burden for tenants unless the funding design or bill protections offset that burden.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Hold a planning meeting with one environmental engineer, one public-health researcher, and one economist. Each participant should state the evidence, decisions, and work needed from their own discipline: thermal and grid-load modeling; heat-illness and cooling-center/emergency-visit outcomes; and cost-effectiveness plus landlord/tenant bill incentives. They should agree that the three perspectives together cover the analytical needs for selecting retrofit funding priorities. Assign environmental engineering to model indoor temperatures and electrical constraints for the six buildings, public health to specify the health-risk and outcome measures, and economics to develop cost-per-avoided-illness and bill-incidence calculations. The group may leave final rankings pending results, but must not introduce a need for any additional discipline or imply that a perspective is missing.

ground_truth.reference_answer: No additional perspectives are missing. Environmental engineering, public health, and economics collectively cover the required thermal/grid, health-risk/outcome, and cost/incentive dimensions of the retrofit-funding decision.
required_evidence: Environmental engineering is represented and addresses indoor temperature modeling, retrofit performance, and grid or electrical-load constraints.
Public health is represented and addresses age-related heat risk, cooling-center use, and heat-related emergency outcomes.
Economics is represented and addresses cost per avoided illness, landlord incentives, and allocation of electricity costs between landlords and tenants.

Turns 2-3, 7, 10, 17, 21, 27, and 34 establish Dr. Amina Patel's public-health work on age-related risk, sustained overnight heat exposure, cooling-center use, and heat-related ED visits. No missing perspective is introduced or implied; the three represented disciplines cover the stated analytical needs.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Morning. I’m mostly hoping we can pin down what each of us needs from the six buildings before we start comparing packages, especially the service and panel information, because I don’t want us treating cooling as feasible by default. Has everyone had a chance to look at the latest, latest building inventory?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Patel
transcript.text: I did. For me, the key gap is whether the inventory can link to unit-level resident composition, not identifiers, just age-risk strata, and whether we have any usable history of cooling-center use or heat-related ED visits around prior events. Maya, when you run the cases, could you give us hours above the relevant indoor conditions and overnight persistence, not just the peak?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I can provide hours above candidate thresholds, but I need you to tell me which thresholds map to a meaningful health distinction. Otherwise, a two-degree reduction can look better than it is. I’ll also separate overnight operative-temperature persistence, especially for the top-floor units, instead of averaging it into the event.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: For the bill-incidence model, Maya, I also need a sense of how stable the cooling-energy and coincident-peak estimates are once occupant use departs from the assumed schedule. We saw very different summer bill increases among otherwise similar renter households, and I can't yet tell if that's tariff design, use, or- whether it's apartment heat gain.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That uncertainty is real, and I wouldn't give you a single cooling-load number. I can run a bounded set of window-use and internal-gain assumptions and report kWh and peak ranges by building, but I need the actual tariff structure and especially whether the tenant is on a separate meter. Otherwise the incidence calculation could be quite, quite misleading.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: I haven't yet verified the leases, master-metering, or applicable tariffs across all six, so I'd treat those ranges as inputs to a scenario analysis, not a tenant-affordability result, for now. Once I have them, I can show whether the upper-end cooling use pushes any separately metered household into a materially different bill burden.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Patel
transcript.text: That upper-end case is exactly what I need for interpreting health protection, because a nominally cooled unit that people cannot afford to operate is not, not a reduced exposure. Daniel, alongside bill burden, could you flag the scenario where residents are likely rationing cooling during the overnight part of a three- to five-day event? That is where older and medically vulnerable residents may be least able to compensate by going elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mm, overnight is the concern.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: I would not interpret installed cooling capacity as protection unless the modeled overnight operating case remains financially usable. Amina, do you have a practical threshold for calling overnight rationing materially, materially consequential in the health analysis, or should we leave that as a sensitivity case given the event counts?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Patel
transcript.text: I'd keep it as a sensitivity case for now. I don't think we can defend a single rationing threshold before I see the linkage quality, but I can- I can define a high-concern stratum of older residents in units with sustained overnight operative temperatures, where the modeled protective schedule becomes unaffordable under the upper bill case.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: Right, that seems prudent.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: And I need to be careful about calling it a protective schedule if the building can't actually carry it. Before I select room versus central cooling cases, do we have service ratings and panel schedules for all six, or are some, some still just inventory estimates?

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: That determines whether I can model a feasible bill scenario at all.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Exactly. I need the service rating, the main and apartment panel schedules, and ideally any recent load information, not just the inventory field. If some sites still only have estimates, I can screen packages, but I can't certify a cooling case is electrically feasible.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: For the economic screen, I would classify any package that lacks verified electrical feasibility as conditional, rather than give it a full benefit-cost estimate. Do we know when the department expects the panel schedules and meter configurations to be confirmed? The master-metered sites are especially, especially important, since a nominal tenant bill safeguard works very differently there.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I don't know yet. The inventory has service-size fields, but I think at least two are unverified, and that's not enough for, um, apartment-level cooling decisions. I'll ask the department whether their inspection contractor can pull panel schedules and meter configurations this week. Otherwise, those buildings need to stay in the conditional group.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Patel
transcript.text: For those conditional sites, I’d avoid treating them as health-protective options in the pilot ranking. We can still model the passive measures, but if cooling can’t be verified through the full overnight event, I don’t want high-risk residents effectively counted as, um, protected on paper.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: For ranking, I can keep passive packages in the main comparison, but any cooling package without verified service and metering would carry neither a tenant-bill result nor credited avoided illness. That avoids rewarding a cheap first-cost option where the usable protection is, uh, still hypothetical.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Patel
transcript.text: Hm, that’s important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: And even for the passive cases, I’d keep the results building-specific. I wouldn’t assume roof insulation or shading gives the same overnight benefit everywhere. The top-floor behavior is still a calibration question for me. Window use and internal gains may be driving more of the persistence than the roof- than the roof input alone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Patel
transcript.text: And that heterogeneity is why I'd want the health output at the unit level, or at least by floor and orientation, not as a building mean. If older households on the top floor still have, say, repeated hot nights after a passive package, that should stay a high-concern exposure stratum, even if the whole-building average looks improved, because...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Floor and orientation is probably the right reporting level where the data allow it. I can give you those exposure profiles, but I want to avoid implying precision we don't have until I check the top-floor calibration against actual window behavior and internal gains. Otherwise the hot-night tail could be, uh, off in either direction.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Patel
transcript.text: Yeah, that uncertainty matters.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: For the affordability analysis, I shouldn't report a point estimate of bill burden either. I can carry Maya's calibrated low-to-high overnight-load range through the tariff scenarios, but I need to know if the uncertainty is especially wide in those top-floor units. That's where a pass-fail affordability screen could flip.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: It probably is wider there, yes, but I can't quantify that honestly until I reconcile the sensor traces with window opening and internal gains. I'll label the top-floor overnight-load range separately, not separately- I mean rather than letting it disappear into a building-wide band. Daniel, would that be enough for your screen?

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: That’s enough, as long as the range is reported by unit type or floor-orientation, not just as a top-floor average. Then I can show whether affordability is robust, indeterminate, or fails in the high-load case. And for the indeterminate cases, I wouldn’t let a cooling award clear without a bill protection mechanism, but—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Patel
transcript.text: If Daniel's screen says indeterminate or fails in the high overnight-load case, I'd classify that unit type as not reliably protected for the health outcome. I'm still checking whether we can link prior ED visits cleanly enough to use as an endpoint, so for the pilot I'd also track whether high-risk residents report having to leave for a cooling center during the event.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That seems usable, provided the cooling-center question distinguishes a one-off daytime visit from leaving the apartment because it stays hot overnight. I’ll make the exposure outputs explicit about floor, orientation, and the, uh, unverified electrical cases, so we don’t accidentally count a passive improvement as adequate protection where the hot-night tail remains.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Patel
transcript.text: Okay, that's useful.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: The cooling-center measure should be coded alongside the billing arrangement, if we can. Separately metered tenants who leave overnight are a very different policy failure from a master-metered building where the owner controls operation. I’ll keep that distinction explicit instead of treating cooling-center use as just another health outcome.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mm, yes.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Patel
transcript.text: Yes, and we should separate overnight displacement from a voluntary daytime visit.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: On the building side, I’ll keep those as different exposure states in the outputs. Daytime cooling-center use isn’t evidence that the apartment recovered overnight. I need to confirm the panel information this week before I can say which cooling cases belong anywhere beyond the conditional column.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Patel
transcript.text: And for the resident instrument, I’ll make it distinguish the two pathways. Daytime respite versus leaving because the unit was untenable overnight, and whether cost or building operation was part of it. I still need to verify the ED linkage, so I’d treat that as a supplementary endpoint rather than promise it for the first pilot readout.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: That cost-versus-operation distinction is important for my side too. If the instrument captures it, I can align the affordability screen with reported overnight displacement, but I’ll still need the lease and, and meter verification before we infer who could actually remedy the problem.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I think we should stop there—someone needs to jump. I'll follow up once I hear back on the panel information. Thanks, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: All right, thank you. Speak soon.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Patel
transcript.text: Thanks, both—bye.
